title: Xi Jinping brings his "A-Game" to Donald Trump’s Washington
gist: Andrew Scobell argues Xi Jinping dominates PRC foreign policy more than any predecessor (including Mao) via 'head-of-state diplomacy': record travel (71 countries, 50+ trips), lavish home hosting, and use of SCO/BRICS stagecraft for domestic legitimacy — though his overseas travel has recently tapered and become highly selective ahead of his second Trump summit in four months.

themes.theme: Xi's personal dominance of PRC diplomacy

insights.claim: Xi Jinping wields more power over PRC foreign relations and is more diplomatically activist than any predecessor paramount leader, including Mao Zedong, who delegated diplomacy to Zhou Enlai.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Outcomes of US-China summits hinge heavily on one man's preferences, raising key-person concentration in geopolitical risk.
insights.quote: Even Mao Zedong was less hands-on diplomatically than Xi and delegated the practice of foreign relations to others, most notably Zhou Enlai.
insights.locator: Xi Jinping wields much more power

insights.claim: The PRC head-of-state post only gained real political and diplomatic significance in the mid-1990s, when the top leader began holding party, state and military top posts simultaneously; the Chinese term is better translated 'chairman' than 'president'.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Explains why summit-level personal diplomacy now carries more weight in Chinese policy than in earlier eras.
insights.quote: The word is usually translated as ‘president’, but a more accurate translation would be ‘chairman.’

insights.claim: Serious PRC head-of-state diplomacy began under Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, but Xi since 2013 upgraded and elevated it far beyond his predecessors, including more pageantry and spectacle.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Summit theatre is a deliberate CCP instrument, so optics-driven announcements may outpace substance.

insights.claim: China now has a highly capable professional diplomatic corps unmatched since 1949, which the author contrasts with an under-strength US State Department and erratic Trump-style foreign policy.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Suggests a structural diplomatic capability edge for Beijing in negotiations with Washington.
insights.quote: The contrast with a below strength US Department of State and an erratic Trump-style foreign policy is hard to overlook.

insights.claim: Jiang visited 71 countries on 39 trips and Hu 69 countries on 50 trips as president; Xi has visited 71 countries on more than 50 trips and is on course to surpass Jiang's record.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Quantifies Xi's diplomatic reach as a baseline for gauging future engagement.
insights.quote: Xi is on course to surpass Jiang’s record, to date having visited 71 countries on more than 50 separate excursions beyond PRC borders.

insights.claim: Xi's September 2026 meeting with Trump is his seventh US trip as head of state and makes him the only PRC president to make two state visits to Washington.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Signals elevated priority Beijing places on stabilizing the US relationship.
insights.quote: will distinguish him as the only PRC president to make two state visits to Washington

insights.claim: Xi's overseas travel has tapered off in recent years, coinciding with intensifying domestic challenges and deteriorating relations with many countries.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Reduced travel is a soft indicator of domestic strain and narrowing diplomatic options.
insights.quote: Yet, in recent years, Xi’s overseas travel has tapered off.

insights.claim: Xi avoids countries where visits might trigger contentious dialogues or hostile protests; his 2024 Europe tour covered only Hungary, Serbia and France.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Xi's itinerary is a readable signal of which European capitals Beijing sees as friendly.
insights.quote: Xi’s 2024 European tour consisted of three countries: two with pro-China governments (Hungary and Serbia) and a third (France) with a head-of-state trying hard to court Xi.

insights.claim: SCO summits and BRICS summits (the latter held in India this year) appear to be obligatory fixtures on Xi's travel calendar.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Confirms Beijing's prioritization of Sinocentric/Global South forums for diplomatic capital.

insights.claim: Since Covid, Xi has devoted more effort to hosting foreign leaders in China, where the CCP can stage-manage every detail from airport arrival onward.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Expect more consequential bilateral deals to be announced from Beijing on choreographed terms.
insights.quote: For Xi, the home court advantage is significant: stage management is much easier in an environment where the CCP can orchestrate every detail

insights.claim: Xi uses world-stage photo-ops and raises the profile of SCO and BRICS to elevate his domestic stature and bolster CCP legitimacy.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Foreign policy outputs serve domestic legitimacy needs, which constrains concessions that would look weak at home.

insights.claim: First lady Peng Liyuan accompanies Xi abroad to an unprecedented degree for a Chinese leader, including 2026 trips to North Korea and Egypt and the Washington visit.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Minor soft-power signal of how Beijing packages leader diplomacy.

insights.claim: In 2017 Trump became the first foreign leader in modern times to dine in the Forbidden City, illustrating Beijing's effort to overawe visitors.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Beijing's personal flattery of Trump is a recurring tactic relevant to summit outcomes.
insights.quote: In 2017, for example, President Trump became the first foreign leader in modern times to dine in the Forbidden City.
